title: Choose the composition for a proposal's page
question: The visual world is settled (the pipeline page's world). This choice is how one proposal's whole dossier is composed. The roll dealt these three; lock one, steer it, or re-roll.

options.label: The Grant Vitals Bench
options.lineage: instrument bench readings — four gauges taken at once
options.thesis: Four vital signs read at a glance — money in, work done, time spent, promises reported — each opening its own evidence in place.
options.viewport: Name, status and the seven-stop lifecycle rail across the top; beneath it four huge typographic readings — 40% funded, 2 of 6 tasks done, day 264 of 365, 0 of 3 targets reported — each over its own thin bar, the off-track one in HC red. Everything else opens underneath without leaving the page.
options.risk: Four readings in a row sits one step away from the stat-tile grid you already rejected; it only earns its place if the figures stay typographic and unboxed.
options.case: Strongest for the daily 'is this grant healthy?' scan. Weakest at showing how the pieces connect to each other — it reports four truths side by side rather than one chain.

options.label: The Grant Instrument
options.lineage: the signed grant agreement itself, as a living document
options.thesis: The page is the instrument: articles for Parties, Term, Consideration, Deliverables and Reporting, each holding live data and reporting its own state in the margin.
options.viewport: An instrument head — the proposal name set large, the status struck as a red seal, term and parties as a preamble — then Article I Parties (ECHO, 1,102,582.21 USD, agreement PRJ-0001) running down one measure, with a numbered article rail in the margin that both navigates and shows each article satisfied, outstanding or breached.
options.risk: Document typography can slow a daily operational scan; the operator's actions (change status, jump to a project) must stay fast inside a form that wants to be read, not worked.
options.case: Strongest at making obligations feel binding and complete — nothing can be quietly missing, because an empty article still prints. Weakest for the manager who wants the number, not the clause.

regions.label: V · Record of amendments — status history

options.label: The Grant Chronology
options.lineage: a single time axis — the money above the line, the work below it
options.thesis: One spine from first concept to final report: transfers above, delivery below, the lifecycle as the line itself — so 'when does the money land against when the work is due' answers itself.
options.viewport: A full-width ribbon across the proposal's term with today marked: above the line the money events (441,032 received 9 Sep, 661,549 pending 27 Apr), below it the project windows, task due dates and target reporting periods; the line itself thickens through the stage the proposal actually sat in longest.
options.risk: Undated records fall off a time axis — and in your live data every one of this proposal's six tasks has no due date. They need an honest berth beside the spine or the page lies by omission.
options.case: Strongest at showing connection: it is the only one of the three where money and delivery are measured against the same ruler. Weakest when a proposal's records are thinly dated.

regions.label: money above the line — transfers scheduled & received
work below the line — projects, tasks, target periods
selected date — full state on that day
